title: Jubilee (Leviticus 25:8–12)
hookLine: every fiftieth year, debts forgiven, land returned, liberty proclaimed

cards: In Philadelphia there's a bell with a crack running up its side. Around the top, cast into the metal, is a line of scripture with the reference right there: Leviticus, chapter twenty-five, verse ten.
It's easy to read the words and think of the American Revolution. Abolitionists later took the bell as their symbol and gave it the name it still has, the Liberty Bell.
But the words are far older, and about something stranger and more radical than independence. A year when everything, in a sense, resets.

teach.b: The law counts in sevens. Every seventh day, rest. Every seventh year, the land rests too.
Then count seven sevens of years, forty-nine, and on the Day of Atonement a ram's horn sounds through the whole land.

Here's the verse on the bell, in the King James Bible: "And ye shall hallow the fiftieth year, and proclaim liberty throughout all the land unto all the inhabitants thereof: it shall be a jubile unto you; and ye shall return every man unto his possession, and ye shall return every man unto his family."
In that fiftieth year, land that had been sold goes back to the family it was first given to.
People who had sold themselves into service because of debt go free and go home.
The reason comes a few verses later: the land is mine, God says, and you're strangers and sojourners with me. Nobody owns anything forever.
The Hebrew name for the year is yovel, a ram's horn, and English jubilee comes from it.

teach.h: DID THEY KEEP IT? NOBODY'S SURE.
teach.b: Did Israel ever keep it? The Bible gives the law but never describes a jubilee year being kept. Nobody can say for sure.
But the idea never went away.

teach.h: PROCLAIM LIBERTY THROUGHOUT ALL THE LAND.
teach.b: In Luke's Gospel, Jesus stands up in the synagogue at Nazareth and reads from Isaiah, about liberty for captives and the acceptable year of the Lord, and some readers hear the jubilee ringing in it.
The Catholic Church still declares holy years called jubilees. And a church-backed campaign took the name Jubilee to press rich nations to cancel the debts of poor countries.

how: Christians hear the jubilee in Jesus' reading at Nazareth, the Catholic Church declares holy years called jubilees, and some churches have used the idea to campaign for debt relief for poor countries.

o: a fiftieth year when land returned and people went free
a yearly harvest feast held at the end of every summer
a royal festival marking fifty years of a king's reign

games.q: what's inside the jubilee — tap the pairs.

s: the words on the Liberty Bell come from Leviticus
"proclaim liberty throughout all the land unto all the inhabitants thereof" — Leviticus 25:10.
historians know for certain Israel kept every jubilee
the Bible gives the law but never describes a jubilee year being kept.
the jubilee was announced with a ram's horn
yovel, the ram's horn, sounded on the Day of Atonement; it gave the year its name.

games.q: your family sold its land to pay debts twenty years ago. the ram's horn sounds for the fiftieth year. what happens?
o: nothing: a sale is a sale.
the land goes back to your family.
you can buy it back at a discount.
games.why: every man returns "unto his possession" and "unto his family". the reason: the land is God's, and nobody owns anything forever.

practice: Think of something someone owes you: ten dollars, a lunch, an apology, a favor never returned, and notice how often you've added it up.
Then picture the ram's horn sounding and the debt going home, not because it didn't matter, but because you'd rather be free of carrying it. If you pray, you can hand the ledger to God.

wordCard.voice: Jubilee. From the Hebrew yovel, a ram's horn. Every fiftieth year in the law, land returned and people freed, liberty proclaimed through the land.

orig.note: Hebrew: a ram's horn, and the year it announced. English jubilee comes from it, by way of Greek and Latin.

carryVoice: Your line: proclaim liberty. It's cast on a cracked bell, and it's far older than the bell. Day four hundred two.
